title: India Issues Ebola Advisory as WHO Declares the Outbreak a Global Health Emergency
excerpt: No cases reported in India yet, but the health ministry is urging travellers from Central Africa to self-monitor for 21 days as the Bundibugyo strain spreads across borders.
body:
India's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare issued a public health advisory on Ebola virus disease on Tuesday, urging caution among travellers who have recently been in Central Africa even as the government confirmed that no cases have been detected within the country.

## A Rare Strain With No Approved Vaccine

The advisory comes as the World Health Organization formally declared the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda a Public Health Emergency of International Concern — a designation reserved for events that pose a risk to multiple countries. The outbreak, driven by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, has now crossed 900 suspected cases with more than 220 suspected deaths, according to the WHO. Unlike more familiar Ebola strains, there is currently no approved vaccine or targeted therapeutic for Bundibugyo, making containment the only viable strategy.

WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Tuesday that the outbreak is "outpacing" the global response, and announced he would travel personally to the DRC to assess conditions on the ground. Responders face severe hurdles: localised conflict in the Ituri Province, where the outbreak is centred, has led to attacks on healthcare facilities and disrupted contact tracing.

## What India's Advisory Asks of Travellers

The ministry's advisory, posted on X and distributed through official channels, specifically targets anyone who has travelled from or transited through an Ebola-affected country within the past 21 days — the maximum incubation period for the virus.

Individuals developing symptoms such as fever, headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding are asked to isolate themselves immediately and inform local health authorities. The government's 24/7 Health Helpline — 1075 — has been designated as the primary point of contact.

"Early reporting can save lives and help prevent the spread of disease," the ministry said.

## Airlines Are Already Responding

The advisory follows a cascade of global travel disruptions linked to the outbreak. KLM, the Dutch carrier, cancelled flights between Amsterdam and Entebbe on Saturday and Monday after several countries imposed entry restrictions on passengers transiting through Uganda. Emirates has advised travellers to check destination entry requirements before flying. In May, an Air France flight from Paris to Detroit was diverted to Montreal after a passenger from the DRC boarded "in error."

The United States has introduced enhanced screening at high-volume airports — including Atlanta and Washington-Dulles — for travellers originating from Central Africa, and has banned entry to non-citizens from the DRC, Uganda and South Sudan. Rwanda and Uganda have also closed their borders.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For the estimated 100,000 Indians living and working across sub-Saharan Africa — including significant communities in Uganda, Kenya and the DRC — the advisory carries immediate practical weight. India's diplomatic missions in the affected region have been instructed to coordinate with local health authorities and provide guidance to Indian nationals.

The outbreak also poses indirect risks to India's pharmaceutical and medical supply chains. India is the world's largest supplier of generic medicines to African nations, and any disruption to logistics corridors could affect both deliveries and the broader public health response on the continent.

## What Comes Next

Health experts say the next two to four weeks will be critical. If the outbreak cannot be contained within the current geographic footprint, the WHO's emergency designation could trigger more restrictive travel measures globally. For India, the focus remains on surveillance and preparedness rather than panic — but the ministry's decision to issue a formal advisory signals that the government is taking the risk seriously.

The WHO has urged countries not to impose blanket border closures, warning that such measures "discourage the transparency that saves lives." But as suspected cases in Brazil and Austria emerge, the pressure on governments to act unilaterally is mounting.
